articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) of the U.S. Department of the Treasury announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This action modifies existing authorizations pertaining to transactions involving Iran.

The specifics of the amendment were not immediately detailed in the announcement, but such changes typically aim to clarify, expand, or restrict the scope of permissible activities under the Iran sanctions program. Businesses and individuals engaging in Iran-related transactions are advised to review the updated license carefully.

This amendment follows a series of recent OFAC actions concerning Iran, including new designations and the issuance of other general licenses and amended FAQs, indicating an active and evolving sanctions landscape for the country.

These amendments aim to clarify compliance obligations for financial institutions and other entities subject to U.S. sanctions. The updated FAQs often address common questions and provide practical examples to assist in navigating complex sanctions requirements.
Staying informed about OFAC's guidance is crucial for maintaining an effective sanctions compliance program and avoiding potential penalties.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea. This multifaceted action also included the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations target individuals and entities involved in activities contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. The removals for Belarus and North Korea suggest a recalibration of sanctions in specific areas, potentially in response to changed circumstances or policy considerations.

The new General Licenses for Iran and Russia, along with updated FAQs, provide guidance on permissible transactions and aim to ensure that humanitarian aid and other authorized activities can continue while maintaining pressure on the targeted regimes.

articles.headline: PAIPA Designations Issued by OFAC with Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

PAIPA targets individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of U.S. intellectual property. The designations aim to protect American innovation and economic security by imposing sanctions on those who engage in such illicit activities.
The accompanying General Licenses are intended to mitigate any unintended consequences of the designations and provide clarity on permissible transactions for affected parties.

articles.headline: OCC Announces October 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including Penalties for BSA Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, highlighting several significant measures taken against financial institutions and institution-affiliated parties. These actions are designed to correct deficient practices and ensure compliance with banking laws and regulations.

Among the key actions, the OCC issued a Cease and Desist Order and a Civil Money Penalty against American Express National Bank for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and violations related to customer due diligence and customer identification programs. The assessed civil money penalty for American Express National Bank is $350 million.

Additionally, the OCC imposed a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association, for similar deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against individuals for embezzling customer funds.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

articles.headline: More than 5,000 die from Ebola in DR Congo's deadliest outbreak
body: Government data shows that more than 10,000 people have contracted the rare virus.

articles.headline: North Carolina voters weigh up Trump's track record on cost of living
body: The BBC's Clive Myrie found voters in the state were asking themselves whether they were better off than two years ago.

articles.headline: Peaceful protests in Germany spiral into violence and looting
body: Thousands joined largely orderly demonstrations earlier in the day, before violence erupted in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.

articles.headline: Watch: Heidi Klum as giant severed hand for Halloween bash
body: The supermodel and TV host provided a gory new shock at her New York event.

articles.headline: Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe
body: More than 320,000 people demonstrated across France against the rising cost of living and poor public services, with clashes between some protesters and police.
